narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 65% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted, signaling weaker academic consistency in the later stages of your degree. Your first-year ranking came next in importance and also pulled the outcome toward failure; a third-decile placement sits well below the sixth-decile average of accepted applicants. These two academic-standing signals outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score of 34 worked in the opposite direction, modestly encouraging a pass prediction, yet it was not strong enough to offset the academic-rank concerns. Other details such as your 3.0 undergraduate GPA (versus 3.23 average), upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time aligned with the majority of accepted students and therefore played little role in the denial.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Targeted preparation in these areas can meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
